title: Carrier Air Wing 5 Field Carrier Landing Practice
description: Pilots assigned to Carrier Air Wing (CVW) 5 participate in field carrier landing practice at Iwo To, Japan. Formerly known as Iwo Jima, Iwo To is an island roughly 750 miles south of Tokyo used by CVW 5 to conduct yearly fighter pilot training and qualifications.
keywords: Carrier Air Wing 5, pilot training, Iwo To, navy, Marine Corps, Japan, F/A-18, CVW 5, super hornet, Iwo Jima
credit: Petty Officer 3rd Class Raymond Diaz III

transcript.text: (speaking in foreign language)
(captain speaking)
- [Voiceover] This small Pacific island,
accessed only by military aircraft,
may look picturesque, but this no vacation spot.
Iwo To, formerly known as Iwo Jima,
and located roughly 750 miles south
of the Japanese mainland, is where in 1945,
American and Japanese forces battled
for control over the island and it's vital airfields.
(aircraft engine)
- Iwo To is our temporary facility,
while we await the identification
of a permanent facility here in Japan
for our field carrier landing practice.
(aircraft engine)
We've been using it for many years,
it gives us an authentic replication
of the environment out at the ship,
and it gives us very good training
for our operations in the carrier qualification,
and then shipboard operations.
- [Voiceover] More than 70 years later,
Iwo To, and it's modern day airfield,
provide pilots from Carrier Air Wing Five
an opportunity to practice and perfect
launching, landing and touch and go qualifications.
- The majority of aircraft you'll see out there
with American markings on them,
will be the Super Hornets from Carrier Airwing Five.
That includes the Echo, Fox and Golf models,
so the fighters and the jammers,
they'll be out there again for about
10 days as the squadrons rotate through their training.
- [Voiceover] Aside from practicing during the day,
pilots also train at night
as part of their training routine.
Pilots practice a total of three
day time practices and three night time practices.
This is half the time pilots
in the U.S. get to qualify, due to the high
operational tempo of the forward deployed carrier.
The squadrons will rotate through training
within a 10 day period.
- So we maintain both our combat effectiveness
for our alliance requirements here in Japan
and the theater requirements.
And also to do it safely, so that we can
protect our families and the Japanese people.
- [Voiceover] Field carrier landing practice
is one of the many ways our forward deployed
naval force stays mission ready.
Reporting from Iwo To, Japan,
I'm Petty Officer Raymond Diaz.
(aircraft engine)
